In regard to the diagnosis, most of the patients presented ECG changes, such as sinus tachycardia [ 123 ], atrial flutter [ 126 ], ST elevation [ 121 , 126 ], or T wave changes [ 120 , 122 ]. A TTE was performed in all the cases and was always abnormal. In patients diagnosed with Takotsubo syndrome, TTE revealed apical akinesis with apical ballooning, hyperdynamic basal LV segments, and a reduced cardiac ejection fraction [ 120 , 121 , 122 , 127 , 129 ]. One case of atypical Takotsubo cardiomyopathy was also described whereby the TTE revealed hypokinesia of the mid inferior and mid anterior septum, mid inferolateral, mid anterolateral, mid inferior and mid anterior wall, sparing the apical and basal segments [ 123 ]. In acute heart failure cases, the wall motion abnormalities were not systematized [ 125 , 126 ]. Chest X-rays uncovered pulmonary congestion, pulmonary effusion, and cardiac dilation, but these were performed only in a few cases [ 123 , 126 ]. A CMR was obtained in the majority of cases, mainly to rule out the diagnosis of ICI-induced myocarditis. It is noteworthy that one patient had concomitant myopericarditis and Takotsubo syndrome following ICI therapy. In this case, the CMR revealed mid-myocardial to subepicardial delayed enhancement (MDE) in the inferior lateral walls, as well as in the apex [ 127 ]. The laboratory analyses (TnI, CK, CK-MB, BNP, and NT-proBNP) were determined in the majority of cases and were almost always elevated, which raised the question of an acute coronary syndrome [ 120 , 121 , 122 , 123 , 125 , 127 , 129 ]. Subsequently, a coronary angiography was performed in the majority of the cases and an acute myocardial infarction was ruled out [ 121 , 122 , 123 , 125 , 126 , 127 , 129 ]. Cardiac catheterization and myocardial biopsies were performed in two patients, which excluded a possible myocarditis [ 120 , 126 ]. The first therapeutic intervention (when ICI-induced side effects were suspected) was the cessation of the incriminated drug. Immunosuppressive therapy with intravenous corticosteroids was initiated and continued with oral prednisone taper when myocarditis was diagnosed [ 127 ] or suspected [ 122 , 125 , 127 , 129 ]. In all cases, guideline-directed heart failure treatment was started with betablockers, ACE inhibitors, and diuretics, as well as IV dopamine and tolvaptan in one severe acute heart failure case [ 126 ]. After the ICI treatment was discontinued and heart failure treatment was initiated, the evolution was favorable in all the cases, with an improvement in the symptoms and the left ventricular ejection fraction [ 120 , 121 , 122 , 123 , 125 , 126 , 127 , 129 ]. 2.5. Acute Coronary Syndrome We analyzed the case reports of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) related to ICI administration, and the time to onset of ACS is 2–365 days, and most of the cases were reported in male subjects with an average age of 67 years, the youngest being 52 yo and the oldest 87 yo. Concerning underlying oncological disease, the cases were reported in patients diagnosed with lung cancer [ 130 , 131 , 132 , 133 , 134 ], melanoma [ 135 ], and renal cell carcinoma [ 136 ], as we have presented in Table 5 . More than 70% of the cases were described as non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), but ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) [ 133 ] and vasospastic angina were also described [ 136 , 137 , 138 ]. The main clinical manifestations of ICI-associated ACS were chest pain and dyspnea; only one case reported no symptoms, and the diagnosis was based on the elevated cardiac biomarkers [ 131 ]. Concerning concomitant autoimmune diseases, one patient developed grade five colitis while being hospitalized for ICI-related myocardial infarction [ 134 ]. Another patient presented related concomitant autoimmune manifestations, namely erythema multiforme, thyroid dysfunction, and interstitial pneumonia [ 131 ], while another case with associated ICI-induced hepatitis was also reported [ 131 ]. The concomitant autoimmune diseases were treated with high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, followed by oral corticosteroids taper. Most of the patients had an abnormal ECG with ST-depression in various territories [ 130 , 135 , 136 ], T-wave inversions [ 132 ], Q-waves [ 116 , 134 ] and ST-elevation [ 132 ]. One case report revealed no ECG abnormalities [ 131 ]. The laboratory analyses (TnI, CK, CK-MB, BNP and NT-proBNP) were determined in the majority of cases and revealed abnormal values, particularly the troponins [ 130 , 131 , 132 , 133 , 134 , 135 , 136 ]. In every case, emergency coronary angiography was performed and revealed significant stenosis or occlusion of the coronary arteries [ 130 , 131 , 132 , 133 , 134 , 135 ], except for the case of vasospastic angina [ 136 ]. Most of the patients underwent a percutaneous coronary intervention with implantation of drug-eluting stents [ 112 , 113 , 114 , 115 , 116 ]. However, one patient with underlying severe CAD was surgically treated with coronary artery bypass grafts (CABG) for the affected arteries [ 135 ]. The patient diagnosed with vasospastic angina was treated with calcium channel blockers and nitrates, and the symptoms gradually disappeared [ 136 ]. All the patients were discharged with chronic myocardial infarction treatment, namely dual antiplatelet therapy, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and statins, except for the patient diagnosed with vasospastic angina [ 136 ]. The evolution of the patients was almost always favorable [ 130 , 131 , 132 , 133 , 134 , 135 , 136 ], except for one patient who died 16 days after stenting due to refractory shock without ACS recurrence [ 134 ]. 2.6. IrAEs Reported in Clinical Trials Between 2017 and January 2022, there were published trials that reported cardiac irAEs following the administration of ICIs, the most common AE being myocarditis. Maio et al. [ 139 ] conducted a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, evaluating the use of tremelimumab as second- or third-line treatment in patients with relapsed malignant melanoma, reporting a multitude of cardiac AE. In the treatment group, one case of myocardial infarction (vs. none in the placebo group) was identified, along with one case of cardiac failure (vs. one in the placebo group) and twelve cases of pericardial effusion (vs. six in the placebo group). A dose-finding and dose-expansion phase 1b trial conducted by Choueiri et al. [ 140 ], regarding the use of avelumab, a PD-L1 inhibitor, in association with axitinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKi), in patients with clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma reported one case of myocarditis diagnosed before the first evaluation of the patients, resulting in the death of the patient. Among the six deaths reported in this study, this was the only one caused by irAEs, with the other five being a result of disease progression. Juergens et al. [ 141 ] assessed the efficacy of durvalumab with or without tremelimumab in combination with platinum-doublet based chemotherapy in several types of malignancies, the most common being NSCLC. There was one reported case of myocarditis, which was confirmed using post-mortem. The ESCORT trial assessed the efficacy of camrelizumab vs. the investigator’s choice chemotherapy regime in advanced or metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. A total of 10 treatment-related deaths were reported, 7 of them for camrelizumab (one with myocarditis) [ 142 ]. Hasson et al. [ 143 ] assessed the safety of reintroducing immunotherapy in patients that survived ICI-induced myocarditis. Three patients were chosen from a total of seven and ICIs were reintroduced under close surveillance and in combination with low dose PO prednisone and cardio-protective therapy (angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, beta-blockers, or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists). One of the three patients exhibited heart failure symptoms which required the cessation of the ICI regiment, while the other two continued treatment with durvalumab and pembrolizumab without irAEs at the time of data cut-off. Limitations of the Study For the moment, a lot of information is emerging from daily clinical practice but must be treated with caution. Considering the lack of full data about patients’ profiles (regarding their cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular history and associated risk factors), further research is needed to fully assess the relationship between ICI and cardiotoxicity. 3. Material and Methods We reviewed all publications from PubMed, Embase, and Medline databases using the terms: (“immunotherapy”[tw] OR “CTLA4”[tw] OR “PD1”[tw] OR “PDL1”[tw] OR “PD-1”[tw] OR “PD-L1”[tw] OR “Immune checkpoint inhibitors”[tw]) AND (“cardiotoxicity”[tw] OR “myocarditis”[tw] OR “Myocardial Infarction”[tw] OR “Heart Failure”[tw] OR “Acute Coronary Syndrome”[tw] OR “Arrhythmias, Cardiac”[Mesh] OR “Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy”[tw] OR “Pericarditis”[tw] OR “Coronary Vasospasm”[tw] OR “Shock, Cardiogenic”[tw] OR “Heart Conduction System”[tw]) NOT (“review”[tiab] OR “meta-analysis”[tiab]). Only human studies from the past five years were selected for screening, including case reports/case series. Duplicates were removed and only articles written in English with the presence of an abstract were reviewed. Reviews, systematic reviews, animal, and in vitro studies were excluded ( Figure 2 ). Figure 2 Flow diagram of the paper selection processes. 4. Conclusions ICI-induced cardiac toxicity comprises a large field of morphological and functional abnormalities, including myocarditis, pericarditis, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and acute coronary syndrome. Despite only a few reports from the first clinical trials involving ICI, many cases were documented in later years. For this review, we identified and collected relevant data from the last five years in the literature in order to highlight the clinical and paraclinical patterns, as well as any therapeutic approaches. Although rare, these adverse events can lead to fatal outcomes, especially in the case of myocarditis. The precise mechanisms are not yet fully elucidated, and consequently, the treatment lacks standardization. Further research is needed for the better stratification of these pathological entities and the proper design for early diagnosis and treatment strategies. documents.title: Diagnostic accuracy of transthoracic echocardiography for acute type A aortic syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is currently recognized as the potential first-line imaging test for patients with suspected acute type A aortic syndrome (AAAS). Direct TTE sign for detecting AAAS is positive if there is an intimal flap separating two aortic lumens or aortic wall thickening seen in the ascending aorta. Indirect TTE sign indicates high-risk features of AAAS, such as aortic root dilatation, pericardial effusion, and aortic regurgitation. Our aim is to summarize the existing clinical evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy of TTE and to evaluate its potential role in the management of patients with suspected AAAS.
METHODS: We included prospective or retrospective diagnostic cohort studies, written in any language, that specifically focused on using TTE to diagnose AAAS from databases such as PubMed, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library. The pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (PLR), negative likelihood ratio (NLR), diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) , and hierarchical summary receiver-operating characteristic (HSROC) curve were calculated for TTE in diagnosing AAAS. We applied Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy (QUADAS-2) tool and Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) quality assessment criteria.
RESULTS: Ten studies (2886 patients) were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of direct TTE signs were 58% (95% CI, 38-76%) and 94% (95% CI, 89-97%). For any TTE signs, the pooled sensitivity and specificity were 91% (95% CI, 85-94%) and 74% (95% CI, 61-84%). The diagnostic accuracy of direct TTE signs was significantly higher than that of any TTE signs, as measured by the area under the HSROC curve [0.95 (95% CI, 0.92-0.96) vs. 0.87 (95% CI, 0.84-0.90)] in four studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that TTE could serve as the initial imaging test for patients with suspected AAAS. Given its high specificity, the presence of direct TTE signs may indicate AAAS, whereas the absence of any TTE signs, combined with low clinical suspicion, could suggest a lower likelihood of AAAS.

However, diagnosis can be challenging due to non-specific symptoms. For a detailed and precise representation of aortic anatomy and issues, specific imaging methods for the aorta are essential. As stated by Isselbacher et al. tools like computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) are crucial in this process. The institutional availability of an imaging modality, an expert imaging physician, and the severity of the patient's condition may also direct modality selection. The widespread presence of CT scanners and their ability to quickly produce clear, high-resolution 3D images have made them a primary choice for evaluating potential aortic issues and vascular procedures, especially in emergent conditions [ 3 ]. TTE offers good availability and the portability of a bedside diagnostic solution. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Association of Echocardiography advocate for the use of TTE as the first-line imaging test for patients with suspected AAAS. This is recommended particularly when the patients' probability of AAAS, based on the Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS), is low [ 4 ]. D-dimer tests possess high sensitivity but are non-specific; thus, patients with positive results require confirmatory imaging [ 5 ]. Due to its accessibility, non-invasiveness, and absence of radiation, TTE has become a favored screening tool [ 6 ]. TTE enables the visualization of the thoracic aorta, pericardium and cardiac valves, to facilitate the identification of both direct and indirect signs of AAAS [ 7 ]. A direct TTE sign is positive if an intimal flap separating two aortic lumens or aortic wall thickening (diameter ≥5 mm) is seen in the ascending aorta. An indirect TTE sign is an echocardiographic finding indicative of high-risk features or complications of AAAS, such as dilatation of the thoracic aortic root (diameter ≥4 cm), pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade, and aortic regurgitation [ 8 ]. Despite its widespread use, there has been limited meta-analytical assessment of the diagnostic performance of TTE. We thus sought to summarize the current clinical evidence regarding the diagnostic test accuracy of TTE and assess the possible role of TTE in the management of patients with suspected AAAS. 2 Material and methods The objective of the present investigation was to aggregate the summary estimates of the diagnostic performance of TTE in detecting AAAS based on existing studies. To achieve this goal, the study adhered to the guidelines outlined in PRISMA, the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy, and the current statements for diagnostic accuracy reviews [ [9] , [10] , [11] ]. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register for Systematic Reviews (registration number CRD42023444560). Two investigators (H.-T. Y. and S.-W. L.) systematically and independently evaluated the relevant published data. 2.1 Data sources and searches We searched extensively and systematically in PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library to identify all pertinent studies on the use of TTE in diagnosing AAAS published before March 12, 2024. To conduct the searches, we utilized medical subject headings (MeSH) and specific keywords to encompass the topics of ultrasonography, echocardiography, AAAS, and the evaluation of diagnostic accuracy [ Appendix Table 1 ]. The reference lists of previous reviews and included original articles were also checked for any additional relevant studies. There were no language restrictions. 2.2 Study selection The studies included in our analysis were either diagnostic prospective or retrospective studies, written in any language, that focused specifically on using TTE to diagnose AAAS. Each of the eligible studies provided enough information to create a 2 × 2 table showing the true-positive, false-positive, true-negative, and false-negative counts. Studies that were anecdotal, case reports, conference abstracts, or animal studies, as well as those that lacked data, used TEE as a diagnostic tool, or employed inappropriate grouping for the final diagnosis were excluded from the analysis. The definitive diagnosis of AAAS was ascertained through various methods, including CTA, MRA, TEE, aortography, and post-mortem examination (autopsy). Two investigators (H.-T. Y. and S.-W. L.) completed the search independently. Using EndNote X9 (Clarivate Analytics, Philadelphia, PA), we conducted the screening process by independently evaluating the titles and abstracts of all studies. Following this initial screening, the same two reviewers independently assessed the full-text articles to determine their eligibility. In cases where there were disagreements, a consensus was reached through discussion and the participation of a third investigator (C.-C. Y.); no automation tools were employed during the review process. 2.3 Data collection and processing The data were recorded independently by two investigators (H.-T. Y. and S.-W. L.) on separate spreadsheets. The data extracted included the following information: the first author, year of publication, country, study design, sample size, setting (emergency department, general ward, or intensive care unit), ultrasound provider, eligibility criteria, reported results, ultrasonography findings, and reference standard test used. If data crucial to the meta-analysis—specifically, information pertaining to sensitivity and specificity—were not present, the corresponding author of the study was contacted for the information by email. In the event of any disagreements, the investigators discussed and resolved them through consensus. If necessary, a third investigator (C.-C. Y.) was consulted. 2.4 Quality assessment An adapted Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2) tool, was used to assess the methodological quality of all included studies and evaluate the risk of bias [ 12 ]. The tool consists of two sections: one for assessing the risk of bias and the other for evaluating concerns regarding applicability. The risk of bias is evaluated across four domains—patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. Concerns regarding applicability were evaluated across three domains, which included patient selection, index test, and reference standard. The qualities of the included studies were independently assessed by two investigators (H.-T. Y. and S.-W. L.). Any discrepancies in the ratings were resolved by reviewing the criteria and consulting a third investigator (C.-C. Y.). 2.5 Statistical analysis We determined both percent agreement and Cohen's kappa for interrater reliability. A 2 × 2 contingency table was utilized for each study to determine the sensitivity, specificity, and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). To visually inspect heterogeneity, we plotted the sensitivity and specificity estimates from individual studies on forest plots and the receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) space. The hierarchical summary receiver-operating characteristic (HSROC) model was then applied to calculate the summary points of several accuracy parameters, including sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratios (PLR) and negative likelihood ratios (NLR), diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) [ 13 ], and their related confidence bounds. To illustrate the precision of summary estimates and variation between studies, we plotted HSROC curve with 95% confidence and prediction regions. We chose the HSROC model for its proven superiority to other methods, utilizing two-level statistical distributions [ 14 ]. It models cell counts in 2 × 2 tables from each study through binomial distributions and logistic transformations, addressing within-study variability. At a higher level, it assumes random study effects to account for heterogeneity in test accuracy beyond sampling variability. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the Chi-squared (χ2) test coupled with the I 2 statistics. We considered heterogeneity to be significant if Cochran's Q p-value was less than 0.1, or when the I 2 value exceeded 50%. All meta-analytic statistics are presented with their corresponding 95% CI [ 15 ]. We conducted subgroup analyses to assess the diagnostic performance of direct and any TTE signs in diagnosing AAAS. These analyses aimed to investigate whether the diagnostic accuracy varied according to several factors, such as publishing year, the number of patients (≥225 or < 225), study design (prospective or retrospective), region (Asia or non-Asia), AAAS prevalence (≥26% or <26%), and ultrasound provider (cardiologist or non-cardiologist). The cutoffs for the number of patients and prevalence were established based on the median values derived from the included studies. Given the significant advances in ultrasound technology over the past few decades, we conducted a subgroup analysis to compare studies published before 2000 and after 2000. We assessed publication bias using Deeks' funnel plot asymmetry test [ 16 ]. Statistical and meta-analyses were conducted in STATA version 17 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX, USA) using several modules: Metandi for summary estimates and HSROC plots, Metadta for forest plots, and Midas for publication bias. When the pooled study number was less than four in subgroup analyses and beyond STATA's processing capability, summary estimates were obtained with Mada package in R version 4.1.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). 2.6 Rating the certainty of evidence To evaluate the effectiveness of the index test for AAAS, we summarized our findings in a tabulated format and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. This method rates the certainty of evidence of each index test across studies, reflecting our confidence in the accuracy of the effect estimate [ [17] , [18] ]. 3 Results 3.1 Search results Our systematic search strategy yielded 5347 articles without duplicates (6146 total). Of these, 48 were selected for full-text review and 10 met all the inclusion criteria. [ Fig. 1 ]. The search in the reference lists of the identiﬁed articles did not yield any more eligible studies. The percent agreement between the two reviewers for article selection was 92%, and Cohen's kappa was k = 0.78. Fig. 1 Flow chart of study identification, screening, inclusion, and exclusion for meta-analysis. Fig. 1 3.2 Study characteristics A total of 2886 patients were included in our meta-analysis. The individual characteristics of the included studies are presented in [ Table 1 ]. The studies’ publication dates span from 1985 to 2023, with a median sample size of 224.5 and a range of 56–839 participants. Geographically, the studies were conducted at three locations in Asia (30%), six locations in Europe (60%), and one location in the United States (10%). Six (60%) of the studies were prospective cohort studies, while four (40%) were retrospective cohort studies. In terms of patient population, six (60%) of the studies investigated the ED population, one (10%) investigated both the ED and ICU populations, and three (30%) investigated patients visiting hospitals in general. With respect to ultrasound providers, one study investigated the diagnostic performance of TTE for AAAS provided by emergency medicine residents, two by emergency physicians, one by cardiologists, one by cardiologists or non-cardiologist physicians (internal or emergency medicine physicians), and five by unspecified sonographers. Regarding applicability, one study (10%) presented high risk of bias in the patient selection domain as it included only patients with ST-segment elevated myocardial infarction [ 19 ]. Fig. 2 3.4 Data analysis 3.4.1 Primary analysis of overall accuracy For our analysis, we collected data from 10 unique studies on four unique signs (one direct sign and three indirect signs) suggestive of AAAS. The prevalence of the disease in our study was 21.4%, ranging from 4.9% to 61.1%. Multiple studies provided sensitivity and specificity data for multiple signs, resulting in 29 measures of sensitivity and specificity being collected. We considered these 29 different studies for our analyses and have presented the results in [ Table 2 ] and [ Appendix Table 3 ]. The most frequently examined application of TTE for detecting AAAS was through the identification of direct TTE signs (i.e., intimal flap or aortic wall thickening) suggestive of AAAS. The pooled sensitivity was 58% (95% CI, 38–76%), while the pooled specificity was 94% (95% CI, 89–97%). The estimated DOR was 22.64 (95% CI, 11.25–45.55). The pooled estimates of PLR and NLR were 9.99 (95% CI, 5.87–16.98) and 0.44 (95% CI, 0.28–0.70), respectively. The second most commonly examined approach was the detection of any TTE signs (i.e., intimal flap, aortic wall thickening, aortic root dilation, pericardial effusion, or aortic regurgitation) which had a pooled sensitivity of 91% (95% CI, 85–94%) and a pooled specificity of 74% (95% CI, 61–84%). The estimated DOR was 27.69 (95% CI, 11.89–64.47). The pooled estimates of PLR and NLR were 3.50 (95% CI, 2.22–5.53) and 0.13 (95% CI, 0.07–0.21), respectively. The detection of root dilatation was also examined, with a pooled sensitivity of 74% (95% CI, 65–82%) and a pooled specificity of 78% (95% CI, 72–83%). In addition, pericardial effusion and aortic regurgitation were reported in four studies with a pooled sensitivity of 35% (95% CI, 26–45%) and a pooled specificity of 92% (95% CI, 89–95%), and a pooled sensitivity of 35% (95% CI, 16–59%) and a pooled specificity of 88% (95% CI, 74–95%), respectively. [ Fig. 3 ] displays the forest plots of sensitivity and specificity for direct signs and any signs, derived from all the included studies. [ Fig. 4 ] presents the HSROC plots for both direct TTE signs and any TTE signs, based on all the studies included. The area under the HSROC curve for direct TTE signs was identified as 0.91 (95% CI, 0.88–0.93), while for any TTE signs, it was 0.92 (95% CI, 0.89–0.94). We downgraded one level. 4 Discussions 4.1 Summary of the main results To the best of our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis assessing the diagnostic accuracy of TTE in diagnosing AAAS. The prevalence of the disease in our studies was 21.4%. The studies consistently showed high specificity for direct TTE signs, with only two of them having specificity lower than 85%. However, the sensitivity was much lower, with only three studies having sensitivity greater than 70%. On the other hand, the studies consistently demonstrated high sensitivity for any TTE signs, with all of them having sensitivity higher than 85%. In contrast, the specificity was lower, with only two studies having sensitivity greater than 75%. One of the reasons is that TTE has exceptionally high sensitivity for pericardial effusion and aortic valve regurgitation, which are present in 46% and 50% of patients with AAD, respectively [ 26 ]. Direct TTE signs demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for identifying AAAS with an area under the HSROC curve of 0.91 (95% CI, 0.88–0.93). Similarly, any signs had an area of 0.92 (95% CI, 0.89–0.94). Following this, the values for root dilatation, pericardial effusion, and aortic regurgitation were 0.83, 0.77, and 0.73, respectively. Our sensitivity analysis suggested that the area under the HSROC curve was not overly reliant on any particular study, reducing concerns over the reliability and generalizability estimates of our results. 4.2 Roles of TTE signs in the diagnosis of AAAS Echocardiography has been established in several large studies to be portable, rapid, and cost-effective in diagnosing AAAS [ 27 ]. Direct TTE signs, which typically represent visual evidence of a tear in the aortic wall or the presence of a false lumen, have high pooled specificity of 94%, indicating that they are highly reliable in detecting AAAS. In patients with suspected AAAS but with a low pretest probability, the decision to proceed with CTA or TEE is notoriously challenging. Misdiagnosis could lead to delayed treatment, complications, or even fatalities. Conversely, unnecessary advanced imaging may expose patients to risks such as radiation, contrast-induced nephropathy, and even esophageal injury in the case of TEE. In this situation, the presence of direct TTE signs acts as a gatekeeper, aiding the decision-making process for a more definitive diagnosis. Indirect TTE signs, which include root dilatation, pericardial effusion, and aortic regurgitation, have varied diagnostic abilities for AAAS. Due to its lower specificity, the use of indirect TTE signs for diagnosing AAAS tends to result in a higher rate of false positives, leading to unnecessary interventions or transfers. Our meta-analysis showed that when combining direct and indirect TTE signs, any TTE signs have a considerably high sensitivity of 91%, indicating the potential for use as an exclusion tool. However, it is essential to emphasize that TTE should not be used as the sole screening tool to rule out AAAS in all patients. According to the ESC guidelines, we can evaluate the clinical probability of AAAS with the ADD-RS, which is based on the presence or absence of 12 risk markers classified into three categories [ 8 ]. The ADD-RS for each patient is calculated by counting the number of categories where one or more risk markers are present. Patients with one or more risk markers in more than one category (ADD-RS > 1) are classified as having a high probability of AAAS, necessitating further evaluation with contrast-enhanced CT scans. When combined with a low probability (ADD-RS < 1) and a negative any sign, the absence of AAAS can be strongly presumed, particularly when an alternative diagnosis is identified. One large multicenter prospective study conducted by Nazerian et al. sought to evaluate the diagnostic value of TTE for AAAS and found that in patients with ADD-RS ≤ 1, a negative TTE sign combined with a negative D-dimer resulted in a failure rate of 0% (i.e., a sensitivity of 100%) [ 21 ]. As shown in our results of meta-analysis and findings from previous studies, TTE combined with integrated strategies might be a useful risk stratification and triage tool for patients with suspected AAAS. Future larger prospective studies are required to validate the diagnostic accuracies of various combinations of strategies for diagnosing AAAS. 4.3 Subgroup analyses Our subgroup analyses revealed differences in study design. For direct TTE signs, in the context of this study, the findings suggest that prospective studies tend to have higher sensitivity but slightly lower specificity compared to retrospective studies. This result might be attributed to factors such as the ability to control for confounding variables, standardized data collection procedures, and study protocols. These elements contribute to the accurate identification of true positive cases. For any TTE signs, the higher sensitivity observed in retrospective studies could be influenced by factors such as larger sample sizes, longer follow-up periods, and access to complete medical records. These factors may contribute to more accurate detection of true positive cases. In a previous study, TTE conducted by specialized cardiologists across various clinical settings showed varying levels of sensitivity (57–88%) and specificity (65–96%) in detecting AAD [ [13] , [28] , [29] , [30] ]. In Cecconi's study, which evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of TTE performed by well-trained cardiologists on 270 patients with suspected AAAS, the sensitivity of direct TTE signs was notably higher at 87% (95% CI, 75–93%). Conversely, a study in which TTE was conducted by emergency physician sonographers reported a sensitivity of only 54% (95% CI 39–68%) [ 7 , 22 ]. However, Nazerian et al. showed that the sensitivity of direct and any TTE signs in the diagnosis of AAAS was not significantly different between cardiologists and non-cardiologists. Our meta-analysis indicated that, in the subgroup analysis, there was no significant difference in the sensitivity and specificity of direct and any TTE signs in diagnosing AAAS between these two groups. While additional research is needed to confirm these observations, our study suggests that frontline physicians, with proper training, could perform TTE effectively when assessing patients with suspected AAAS. Moving forward, there is a pressing need to strengthen TTE educational programs for frontline physicians. Such initiatives might include a standardized TTE curriculum and the incorporation of simulation-based training, which could potentially ensure timely and accurate diagnoses of AAAS. 4.4 Strength of the review A recent meta-analysis explored the diagnostic accuracy of TTE in identifying proximal aortic dissection and suggested that TTE should be routinely used for triage [ 31 ]. However, the definition of the target population varied among the included studies. While the authors intended to evaluate the diagnostic value of proximal aortic dissection, their analysis encompassed studies on AAD, IMH, and PAU. Their use of the random effects model to synthesize summary estimates deviated from the reporting guideline's recommendation, which favors multivariate models [ 32 ]. Some studies in their analysis only featured a case group, and lacked a control group, casting doubt on the accuracies of the pooled sensitivity and specificity. The study did not specify the statistical model used for calculating the area under the SROC curve, and the SROC plot presented appeared questionable. Furthermore, their meta-analysis indicated low heterogeneity for the overall results with a Higgin's I 2 of zero, a result that contrasts sharply with our findings and seems counterintuitive. The validity and applicability of our study have been considerably augmented by various methodological strengths. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we: (1) employed the HSROC model in accordance with reporting guidelines to pool summary estimates for each TTE sign; (2) directly compared the diagnostic statistics of the direct TTE sign and any TTE sign, offering valuable insights for clinical implications; (3) executed a comprehensive and duplicated systematic search without any language restrictions; (4) due to significant heterogeneity among the studies, carried out additional subgroup analyses; (5) conducted a sensitivity analysis to ensure the robustness of our results. 4.5 Limitations of the review Our research has several limitations. First, inherent to any systematic review is the potential for omission of relevant articles. Despite our rigorous search strategy and strict adherence to protocol, we cannot fully eliminate this risk. Second, while our results indicated no significant difference between cardiologists and non-cardiologists in the diagnostic accuracy for AAAS, some studies in our review not included in the subgroup analysis lacked detailed descriptions of the expertise and experience of the TTE providers. This omission could potentially bias the final results. Third, our analysis predominantly involved emergency department patients without detailed reporting on illness severity or clinical status, such as hemodynamic status and mechanical ventilation. This absence of data may limit the generalizability of our results. Fourth, we compared the performance of direct and any TTE signs, focusing exclusively on studies with simultaneous measurements. While direct comparison offers advantages in addressing potential confounding arising from study characteristics, the limited number of comparative studies included may restrict the interpretability of the results. Finally, we could not compare the outcomes between patients who underwent TTE examination and those who did not, due to the limited number of studies available for meta-analysis and this comparison being beyond the scope of our review. 5 Conclusions Our study proposes that TTE could be considered as the initial imaging method in the diagnostic process for patients with suspected AAAS. Given its high specificity, the presence of direct TTE signs acts as a rule-in test, providing a more straightforward path to establishing a definitive diagnosis. Moreover, combining the absence of any TTE sign with low clinical suspicion could offer a more secure basis for excluding AAAS. Future research is needed to validate the diagnostic accuracies of different combinations of TTE signs and clinical scoring systems, aiming to enhance patient outcomes.
